prompt: In a POSCAR, what does line 2 (for example 5.43) do?

options.text: It multiplies all the lattice vectors, so the cell is scaled by that factor
options.why: That is the scaling factor: lengths in the next three lines are multiplied by it.

options.text: It is the number of atoms in the cell
options.why: The atom counts are on their own line, after the element symbols.

options.text: It is the cutoff energy in eV
options.why: The cutoff is set by ENCUT in the INCAR, not in the structure file.

hints: Look at what follows line 2: three lattice vectors.
Which quantity would you rescale to make the whole cell bigger?

visual.caption: The POSCAR is one of the four inputs VASP reads.
visual.alt: Boxes for the four input files on the left feeding a box called VASP, which feeds the output files on the right.

prompt: The POSCAR lists the elements Si then O, but your POTCAR was built O then Si. What happens?

options.text: VASP may still run, but each atom gets the wrong dataset, so the results are wrong
options.why: VASP pairs datasets and species by position, so a swapped order gives a valid-looking run for the wrong system.

options.text: VASP sorts them out by name
options.why: The file order is what counts; nothing re-matches them by name.

options.text: The run is slower but correct
options.why: The error is in the physics, not in the speed.

hints: Where does VASP learn which dataset belongs to which atom type?
Think of what grep TITEL POTCAR is for.

visual.caption: POSCAR and POTCAR must list the elements in the same order.
visual.alt: Boxes for the four input files on the left feeding a box called VASP, which feeds the output files on the right.

prompt: A POSCAR says Direct and gives 0.25 0.25 0.25 for an atom. Where is the atom?

options.text: A quarter of the way along each lattice vector from the origin
options.why: Direct coordinates are fractions of the three lattice vectors.

options.text: 0.25 angstrom from the origin along x, y and z
options.why: That would be Cartesian coordinates, which are in angstrom.

options.text: At the centre of the cell
options.why: The centre is 0.5 0.5 0.5.

hints: What does Direct mean for the unit of the numbers?
Compare with the cell centre.

visual.caption: The POSCAR holds the atom positions.
visual.alt: Boxes for the four input files on the left feeding a box called VASP, which feeds the output files on the right.

prompt: After a relaxation, which file holds the final geometry in POSCAR format?

options.text: CONTCAR
options.why: CONTCAR is rewritten after every ionic step and holds the latest structure.

options.text: OSZICAR
options.why: OSZICAR is a short log of energies, not a structure file.

options.text: CHGCAR
options.why: CHGCAR holds the charge density, not the atom positions.

hints: Which file has a name that sounds like a continuation of POSCAR?
Which file would you copy to POSCAR for the next stage?

visual.caption: CONTCAR is one of the output files; copy it to POSCAR for the next stage.
visual.alt: Boxes for the four input files on the left feeding a box called VASP, which feeds the output files on the right.

prompt: Why do many groups use Gamma-centred meshes for hexagonal cells?

options.text: A Gamma-centred mesh keeps the lattice symmetry, while a shifted mesh can break it
options.why: A mesh that always contains the zone centre respects the point-group symmetry.

options.text: Gamma-centred meshes always have fewer points
options.why: The number of points depends on the subdivisions, not the centring.

options.text: Monkhorst-Pack meshes are not allowed in VASP
options.why: They are allowed; they can just break the symmetry on some lattices.

hints: Which point does a Gamma-centred mesh always include?
What does a shifted grid do to the symmetry of the lattice?

visual.caption: A Gamma-centred mesh always includes the zone centre.
visual.alt: A square grid of k-points in the Brillouin zone, with the point at the centre marked or not depending on the centring.

prompt: Which KPOINTS layout is right for a band structure along a path?

options.text: Line mode, with the start and end of each segment
options.why: Line mode fills in the points between the ends of each straight segment.

options.text: A single automatic mesh with 1 1 1
options.why: That is one point, not a path.

options.text: No KPOINTS file at all
options.why: Without a file VASP uses a default mesh, not a path.

hints: A band plot follows straight lines between special points.
Which layout lets you list segment ends?

visual.caption: The KPOINTS file sets the sampling.
visual.alt: Boxes for the four input files on the left feeding a box called VASP, which feeds the output files on the right.

prompt: How should you decide whether your k-mesh is dense enough?

options.text: Compare several meshes, such as 4x4x4, 6x6x6 and 8x8x8, until the energy stops changing by about 1 meV per atom
options.why: Convergence is judged by the energy settling, and metals need more points than insulators.

options.text: Use the smallest mesh that runs
options.why: A mesh that runs can still be unconverged.

options.text: Trust one mesh if the run finished
options.why: A finished run says nothing about the sampling error.

hints: One number cannot show a trend.
What do you compare between meshes?

visual.caption: A denser Gamma-centred mesh samples the zone more finely.
visual.alt: A square grid of k-points in the Brillouin zone, with the point at the centre marked or not depending on the centring.

prompt: Which file can build a k-mesh when no KPOINTS file is given?

options.text: The INCAR, through the KSPACING tag
options.why: KSPACING lets VASP make the mesh from a spacing, without a KPOINTS file.

options.text: The POTCAR
options.why: The POTCAR holds pseudopotential data, not sampling.

options.text: The OSZICAR
options.why: OSZICAR is an output log, not an input.

hints: The answer is an input file that holds tags.
Which tag name contains the word space?

visual.caption: The INCAR is an input file; KSPACING sets the mesh from it.
visual.alt: Boxes for the four input files on the left feeding a box called VASP, which feeds the output files on the right.

prompt: You leave NSW out of an INCAR. What kind of run do you get?

options.text: A single-point calculation, because the default number of ionic steps is zero
options.why: Many defaults depend on other tags; with no ionic steps, IBRION also falls back to -1.

options.text: A relaxation with 100 steps
options.why: A relaxation needs NSW above zero.

options.text: VASP refuses to start
options.why: A missing tag is not an error; it takes its default.

hints: What does an omitted tag take?
What does NSW count?

visual.caption: With NSW equal to zero there is one electronic calculation and no ionic moves.
visual.alt: A row of boxes for ionic steps; with zero ionic steps a single box is highlighted.

prompt: You misspell a tag in the INCAR. How can you check what VASP actually used?

options.text: Read the parameter echo at the top of the OUTCAR
options.why: The echo lists the values VASP used, so a misspelled tag shows up as missing.

options.text: Look at the file size of the INCAR
options.why: The size says nothing about whether a tag was recognised.

options.text: A misspelled tag always stops the run with an error
options.why: It may be ignored silently, which is why you check.

hints: Which output file repeats the settings?
Where does the OUTCAR start?

visual.caption: The OUTCAR echoes the settings VASP used.
visual.alt: Boxes for the four input files on the left feeding a box called VASP, which feeds the output files on the right.

prompt: A relaxation INCAR sets EDIFFG = -0.005. What does the negative sign mean?

options.text: Stop when every force is below 0.005 eV per angstrom
options.why: A negative EDIFFG is a force criterion; a positive one is an energy-change criterion.

options.text: Stop when the energy change is below 0.005 eV
options.why: That is what a positive EDIFFG means.

options.text: Ignore ionic convergence
options.why: The sign chooses the criterion; it does not switch it off.

hints: Which quantity does a negative EDIFFG compare?
Forces are in eV per angstrom.

visual.caption: Forces fall step by step; the relaxation stops when they pass below the band.
visual.alt: Curve of the largest force falling over ionic steps on a logarithmic axis, with a horizontal band at the force tolerance.

prompt: Why must MAGMOM have one value per atom, in POSCAR order?

options.text: Each value is the starting moment of the atom at that position in the file
options.why: The list is matched to atoms by position, so order and count matter.

options.text: VASP averages the list over all atoms
options.why: It uses the individual values; no averaging happens.

options.text: The order does not matter if the sum is right
options.why: The moments are assigned atom by atom, so the order does matter.

hints: How does VASP know which number goes with which atom?
What does a short list do?

visual.caption: MAGMOM in the INCAR follows the atom order of the POSCAR.
visual.alt: Boxes for the four input files on the left feeding a box called VASP, which feeds the output files on the right.

prompt: Which command shows the recommended cutoff of each dataset without opening the file?

options.text: grep ENMAX POTCAR
options.why: ENMAX is the recommended cutoff in each dataset header, and grep prints only that line.

options.text: grep ENCUT POTCAR
options.why: ENCUT is an INCAR tag; the dataset header uses ENMAX.

options.text: cat POTCAR
options.why: That prints the whole file, which you should not do or share.

hints: Which header name is the dataset's own cutoff?
You want only the header line.

visual.caption: The POTCAR is one of the four inputs.
visual.alt: Boxes for the four input files on the left feeding a box called VASP, which feeds the output files on the right.

prompt: What is the safe way to share your setup with a collaborator?

options.text: Share the TITEL lines or dataset names, and let them use their own licence
options.why: The POTCAR is licensed and may not be redistributed, but its dataset names are fine to share.

options.text: Email the POTCAR file
options.why: The licence forbids redistribution.

options.text: Paste the first 50 lines into a forum post
options.why: Any part of the file is licensed content.

hints: What is licensed: the names or the files?
What do collaborators need to rebuild it?

visual.caption: The POTCAR is an input file you build yourself from a licensed library.
visual.alt: Boxes for the four input files on the left feeding a box called VASP, which feeds the output files on the right.

prompt: What does ZVAL in a POTCAR header tell you?

options.text: The number of valence electrons of that dataset per atom
options.why: ZVAL counts the electrons treated explicitly; summing over atoms gives the electron count.

options.text: The cutoff energy in eV
options.why: That is ENMAX.

options.text: The atomic mass
options.why: That is POMASS.

hints: Z stands for charge and VAL for valence.
Which header value changes with _pv or _sv?

visual.caption: The POTCAR header lists the valence electrons.
visual.alt: Boxes for the four input files on the left feeding a box called VASP, which feeds the output files on the right.

prompt: What does a _pv or _sv variant of a dataset change?

options.text: It treats semicore states as valence, which costs more and is often more accurate
options.why: The variants trade accuracy against cost by adding electrons to the valence.

options.text: It switches the functional from PBE to LDA
options.why: LEXCH names the functional; the suffix does not change it.

options.text: It makes the cutoff smaller
options.why: The variants usually need the same or a higher cutoff.

hints: What do p and s refer to in the name?
More valence electrons means what for cost?

visual.caption: The POTCAR variant is chosen when you build the file.
visual.alt: Boxes for the four input files on the left feeding a box called VASP, which feeds the output files on the right.

prompt: Which file is the most valuable one to restart from, and why is it large?

options.text: WAVECAR, because it holds the wavefunctions
options.why: Starting from converged wavefunctions cuts the number of electronic steps, but they take a lot of space.

options.text: OSZICAR, because it is the log
options.why: It is small and cannot be read back as a starting point.

options.text: CONTCAR, because it holds the density
options.why: CONTCAR holds the geometry only.

hints: Which file name sounds like wavefunctions?
Which is binary?

visual.caption: WAVECAR is one of the output files you can restart from.
visual.alt: Boxes for the four input files on the left feeding a box called VASP, which feeds the output files on the right.

prompt: You set LCHARG = .FALSE. in the SCF run. What goes wrong in a later band run with ICHARG = 11?

options.text: There is no CHGCAR to read, so the band run has nothing to start from
options.why: ICHARG = 11 reads the charge density the SCF wrote.

options.text: Nothing, because the band run recomputes it
options.why: ICHARG = 11 keeps the density fixed; it does not recompute it.

options.text: The band run reads WAVECAR instead
options.why: ICHARG = 11 reads CHGCAR.

hints: Which tag controls whether CHGCAR is written?
What does ICHARG = 11 read?

visual.caption: The band run reads the CHGCAR the SCF wrote.
visual.alt: Three stages in a row, relaxation then SCF in the same folder then a band or density-of-states run, with the file that travels along each arrow.

prompt: Which file would you use to plot projected bands?

options.text: PROCAR, written when LORBIT is 10 or more
options.why: PROCAR holds band and orbital projections at every k-point.

options.text: IBZKPT
options.why: That is the list of irreducible k-points.

options.text: XDATCAR
options.why: That is the trajectory of positions.

hints: Projections need LORBIT.
Which file name starts with PRO?

visual.alt: Boxes for the four input files on the left feeding a box called VASP, which feeds the output files on the right.

prompt: A job stopped early. Which file still holds the latest geometry?

options.text: CONTCAR, because it is rewritten after every ionic step
options.why: The geometry is saved at each step, so an early stop still leaves it.

options.text: POSCAR, because VASP updates it
options.why: POSCAR is an input that VASP does not change.

options.text: DOSCAR, because it holds the structure
options.why: DOSCAR holds the density of states.

hints: Which file is rewritten as the run goes?
Is the input file ever touched?

visual.caption: CONTCAR is updated after each ionic step.
